title: Bible Bowl Hammer
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
BARMATRIX Q#: 14685_bible_bowl_hammer

Peter and Paul were watching a live-streamed Bible trivia championship at Peter’s apartment. Upset by a ruling from the moderator, Paul threw a ceramic mug at Peter’s television, cracking the screen. Enraged, Peter picked up a nearby hammer and hit Paul on the head with it. Paul died from the blow.

The crimes below are listed in descending order of seriousness. In a jurisdiction that follows common law principles, what is the most serious crime of which Peter could properly be convicted?
call: The crimes below are listed in descending order of seriousness. In a jurisdiction that follows common law principles, what is the most serious crime of which Peter could properly be convicted?
rightExplanation: A is correct. Peter intentionally struck Paul on the head with a hammer, and Paul died from that blow. The call asks for the most serious crime of which Peter could properly be convicted. Gold Key: common-law murder is not limited to a purpose to kill; it can also rest on intent to cause serious bodily injury when death results. Silver Key: when the answer choices are a descending seriousness ladder, once the top rung is legally available, every lower rung becomes not responsive to “most serious.”

c3.label: CUT
c3.text: No choice can be cleanly cut before the tiny anchor. All four are offense labels.

c3.label: CALL / Gold Key
c3.text: Apply the serious-bodily-injury murder anchor. A becomes legally available.

c3.label: CUT after anchor
c3.text: B, C, and D are lower-rung answers and therefore not responsive to “most serious.”

studentScript: Call says most serious. Ladder starts with murder. Hammer to head plus death triggers the Gold Key: serious-bodily-injury murder. Take A. B, C, and D are lower rungs.

A.signal: Top rung in the ladder becomes available once the serious-bodily-injury murder anchor is applied.
A.lawyer: Common-law murder can be supported by intent to cause serious bodily injury when death results; the hammer-to-head blow supports that theory.

B.signal: It answers a possible mitigation/lower-offense question, not the most-serious-crime call.
B.lawyer: Voluntary manslaughter may be argued if adequate provocation is found, but a jury could reject mitigation and convict of murder.

C.signal: It names a lower homicide category after the top rung is available.
C.lawyer: Even if a lesser homicide theory could be charged, murder is the most serious available conviction.

D.signal: It names a lower offense and ignores the homicide result and highest-rung call.
D.lawyer: Assault is lower than murder and does not answer the most-serious-crime question.

goldKeys.statement: At common law, murder is not limited to intent-to-kill. A killing can be murder when the defendant intended serious bodily injury and death resulted.
goldKeys.trigger: A deliberate blow with a dangerous object to the head followed by death.
goldKeys.unlocks: The voluntary-manslaughter trap after an angry serious-injury blow.
goldKeys.authority: Common-law malice aforethought; serious/grievous bodily harm theory.

silverKeys.statement: When the call says the crimes are listed in descending seriousness, pick the highest rung that is legally available; lower rungs can be true and still lose.
silverKeys.trigger: Call phrase: 'most serious crime' plus descending-order answer choices.
silverKeys.unlocks: Lower-offense trap in a seriousness ladder.

remediation.title: Highest Available Rung
remediation.signal: Call asks for most serious crime and choices are offense ladder.
remediation.studentMove: Use a Gold Key to see whether the top rung is legally available; if yes, lower rungs are not responsive.
remediation.tinyRule: Lower offenses may be true but still wrong when the call asks for the most serious proper conviction.
remediation.trap: Stopping at voluntary manslaughter because the anger feels mitigating.
